messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: LYNX DISPERSAL
parts:
1. See the literature on dispersal. These may help you find other sources:

Fujiwara, M., Anderson, K. E., Neubert, M. G. and Caswell, H. (2006). On the estimation of dispersal kernels from individual mark--recapture data. Environmental and Ecological Statistics 13, 183-197

Nathan, R., Klein, E., Robledo-Arnuncio, J. J. and Revilla, E. (2012). Dispersal kernels: review. In: J. Clobert et al. (eds) Dispersal Ecology and Evolution. Oxford University Press. Pp. 187-210.

2. Dispersal kernels are almost always fat-tailed; so we expect exponential to be the better 'canned' option. Even that is only borderline fat-tailed.
3. Do not expect too much of the models. I haven't yet seen an application of SECR/SCR where I really trust the results for dispersal.
Murray

P.S. I hope your caps topic doesn't start a trend

messages.subject: Re: LYNX DISPERSAL
parts:
Dear Murray,
I'm back in this analysis.
Read the literature you recommended and tried to run a negative exponential Kernel with JSSAsecrlCL model, it took ages.
I just realized what's the problem: my cameras actually change, in number and position, primary occasion after primary occasion and the mask I created from such trapfile is of course crazy. 
Dealing with this issue seems not easy and so I wanted to know your opinion about it. Considering you told me not to expect too much from dispersal modeling, can't I just stop and trust JSSAlCL estimates (which are quite satisfactory in my opinion)? Would estimates (phi and lambda) be much different using JSSAsecrlCL?

Thanks for your time,
Best, 
Stefano

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: LYNX DISPERSAL
parts:
Hi Stefano
It should be possible to solve your mask problem. In my experience -
1. When a non-spatial model is fitted to data from spatial sampling, in general the estimates of phi will be slightly negatively biased (1-4%, which may or may not be acceptable depending on your application), and the nonspatial estimates of lambda will be essentially unbiased.
2. Things get worse if the spatial extent of sampling changes over time (exposing different sets of animals); then lambda-hat from the non-spatial model may be very biased (see e.g. Hines & Nichols 2002 J Applied Statistics) but the spatial estimates are OK.

I don't know if that applies in your case.

Murray

parts: The mask needs to be large enough that it includes every animal that might be detected, even if it is at risk for only one primary session. You can get that by running ch <- join() to create a pooled capthist object and then running mask <- make.mask(traps(ch), buffer = xxx, nx = yyy, type = 'trapbuffer') where xxx is appropriate to lynx and yyy is some number >= 32 (determines the coarseness of the mask). The result may still be crazy - you will have to see!
